You will have 50 minute puzzle levels that you have to replay from the beginning if you make one wrong move. You will have teleporter mazes designed by a colorblind schizophrenic because all of the portals are identical but do different things. Bosses that "you just had to know to not bring a slow comp to, try again next time" after struggling through 20 minutes of penis flattening to get to in the first place. You will want to make like AR-15 and explode after about an hour of trying to speedrun an event during its last day, because you procrastinated too much but still want the clear. And finally, you will fatfinger a node on the map and debate ending it all realizing you now have to redo 20 minutes of slow and shitty gameplay because the devs haven't put in a rewind button for the overworld maps in the 9 years the game has been out.

But god damn, can Chinese Kojima and his minions write up a very compelling world and spy thriller story.

[b]TLDR[/b]: do you like girls? do you like playable bosses? do you like mechs? do you like supremacy type games? do you like a story where the MC doesn't speak in text boxes and acts like, you know, a character? if anything here appeals to you, play girls' frontline.

I started playing around half a year ago. i'm a professional story-skipper (and yet, i watched a 4-hour story recap on youtube), and i've been enjoying what this game has to offer, and i can certainly say that girls' frontline is my favorite gacha game at the moment (it used to be arknights, but i'm starting to get burnt out after a year of playing it, and yes, playing it, i'm 2 levels away from max level).

This game quite literally has everything i could've wanted for in a tacticool kind of game:
nameless (robo-)girl soldiers, check. (i'm so glad there isn't a "trololo" or a "klukaka", only "AK-Alfa" and "HK 416")

equipment, check (i discovered yesterday that some t-doll-exclusive equipment even has bonus effects in addition to bonkers stats that make them unique).

limit breaker system, check (and i thought arknights' modules were good...until they started giving new units modules on their release day).

playable bosses, check (straight up a huge draw, and these actually ACT like bosses when you use them, unlike a certain fire dragon from Nikke...).

and most importantly; a useable mech, check (i haven't unlocked it yet, but i saw videos of it, and it looks AWESOME. i can't understand why game devs won't try having mechs in their games like in titanfall).

Unlike the stinking premium currency (that exists, but only for costumes. best business practice) that genshit introduced, here you use your naturally-gained resources to get t-dolls, the chances of getting a specific 5 star is still RNG (i still can't get AK-12, and G11 after a month of trying for them with specific recipes i got), as annoying as it is, i can't complain much, since the game is... VERY generous with it's 2-4 stars, and you also get the AR team (arguably the second strongest team when maxed) completely for free by progressing story chapters.

There is also this thing called a "mod system". some T-dolls are allowed to be upgraded further than their limit using special currency (obtainable through daily sweep and other means), upping their stats and rarity on MOD I, more stats, and getting a new skill on MOD II, and finally, more stats, getting a completely new artwork (FOR FREE! fuck you, Nikke and your shitty gacha skins), and also free exclusive equipment i believe (currently, i only have SPAS-12 at MOD III, because her waist-mounted shields are really cool-looking).

Also the default lobby theme makes me feel nostalgic despite playing this game for half a year.

I’ve played countless gacha games, from the most popular ones to the most obscure titles out there, but this one was the only game that truly hooked me for more than seven years. From my Kancolle days back in 2016, and catching my interest on the game with Deep Dive on the CN server in 2017, then the long wait for the global server, the never-ending anticipation for Reverse Collapse, the release of Neural Cloud, and finally Exilium.

There were highs and lows, shifts in quality, and pointless drama in all those years. With a small community but with lot of passion: the artists who made fanart of the popular ones and the more niche ones, the guide creators who carried the global server for years because global cannot read at all, and the collective madness of the lore-compilers who helped everyone grasp the massive universe behind the game.

This game changed me, both as a player and as a person, and I’m truly grateful to the developers and the community that kept it alive through all these years.

THE OG of OG "gacha" games. Post-Genshin Impact, you don't see gacha mechanics like these anymore, this was from a different era, a much simpler and friendlier one. All craftable dolls are available all of the time using the different "recipes" to target specific doll types, no "limited banner" nonsense here. The same resources you use to play the game are the same ones you use to "roll" for new dolls. Don't fret though, your income of such resources is plentiful and you can roll hundreds upon hundreds of times every month once your account gets going. NEVER PAY TO ROLL, YOU ARE ACTIVELY DISCOURAGED FROM DOING SO WITH HOW ABYSMAL THE EXCHANGE RATES ARE. You could say this game is "F2P encouraged" in that regard. All you'll ever be paying for is the abysmal skin gacha if you care about skins, but there are plenty in the store you can buy directly if you wish too.

This game is incredibly casual and cozy, but that's coming from essentially a day 1 player, I have so much excess of everything that it's all meaningless to me, and therefore I can't give a reliable opinion on what the new player experience would be like this far into the game's lifespan now that the story is "over" (even though there are a few new story events being made but the most recent one on JP should actually be the last major one now). What this game's experience will be like after it reaches "maintenance mode", I have no idea. I assume they'll keep it running for a long while since it isn't that popular and the server costs probably aren't anything crazy.

What you'll be playing this game for is the story, which is a whole different beast in and of itself from anything else on the market. I can't even begin to describe it but just know that the anime does not do it justice in the slightest and should be avoided entirely (unless it's the "GFL Healing Chapter" mini series with the chibis, that's absolute cinema, GIVE US HEALING SEASON 3!!!). The first few chapters in the game are nothing to write home about, but once it picks up, it picks up. There's a reason why this game's story has a reputation.

That being said, should you experience the story through this game? I'm not entirely sure. The whole thing is online for you to read at your leisure and you don't have to deal with actually playing the game itself if you don't want to, and in that regard, the game can be quite "jank" and cryptic at times with how to beat stages to the point of it being frustrating if you're doing it on your own for the later event stages. Thankfully, there are plenty of guides online if you don't want to deal with it, but if you already don't want to deal with it, then why play the game to begin with? I've only stuck around as long as I have because I started playing when I did and to collect all of the cute dolls. It's a low maintenance habit I don't mind doing. The game is very forgiving in regards to how much you'll actually "need" to play it and FOMO. Only collab events are the ones you need to be afraid of having content never coming back, but if you're a new player picking the game up today, there's nothing you can really do about that anyway. There are no "gamebreaking" rewards and units that come from collab events, so you can rest easy in that regard.

The combat is nothing to write home about and it's essentially an auto battler outside of a few late game boss fights (where you admittedly have to put in actual effort and the "tech" you can do is actually quite in depth, but there are just as many "cheese" strategies as well), but is it worth that effort? By all means, you can enjoy what this game offers without having to actually play it. GFL's always had a dedicated niche fanbase for a reason.

All I can say is, give the game a try if you want, but don't feel bad if you don't enjoy it. The game is essentially risk free, and you shouldn't feel pressured into spending any money outside of QoL once you can confirm for yourself that you actually like playing it. There is no P2W here as far as I'm concerned.

Good luck, Shikikan.

played this game for years on mobile/emulator so needless to say you can sink hours into it. if you're reading this you probably already know whether you will play this or not so let me just give some pointers to new players instead.

there are crapton of waifus to choose from and each of them has their own personality so you will find your waifu fo sho. as far as gameplay is concerned this is a strategy game and each mission is played on a map of nodes - you either have to capture specific ones or kill a specific target for the most part (game itself is very good at describing mechanics so this is as deep as i'm gonna go into this). there are plenty of missions to go through and there is an actual story which is not half bad so you will get your money's worth.

my recommendation for new players would be to boot up the game, go to friends section and invite everyone until your friendslist is full so you can collect batteries from them. use batteries to upgrade your base facilities. in paralel try to speedrun campaign so you can unlock all of the logistics missions and start running logistics asap so you have resources to craft stuff. focus on leveling ar team as they will carry you through the game. level dolls either through auto-battles or corpse dragging (look it up). also, do exploration missions because that is the quickest way to get combat reports for leveling dolls. long story short just fugg around with the ui and check out what's what.

as far as gacha system is concerned dare i say it's quite fair. you can do your rolls even if you play for free. you will progress slower in game but it's possible to play it for free in its entierity. if you want to support the server there is a sort of 'monthly dlc' which gives you a skin for one random doll and bunch of resources BUT you have to actually play the game to get them.

i think that's all - it's a good game. if you like gunz and anime tiddies you will enjoy this for sure.

However, while it wasn't terribly difficult to get back to, it was terribly confusing.  So, for those returning players who started with Google Play accounts and are confused af - your Gmail login that you use with the Play store is the email you type in when you start up the Steam version of GFL.  If you remember what password you made up for this game, great, but if you're like me and couldn't remember even making a password for the game, just log in with your Google ID via a phone that's already connected to your Google Play account and basically go through the "Forgot Password" process using your Gmail.  Ta dah, you can log into Steam GFL.
In all seriousness, played this a long time ago when it first came out - watched it grow and evolve and change over the course of a few years, eventually uninstalled it and stopped playing shortly after they started the gacha with the former big bads in the story.  I'll try to be detailed without being too long:
- Yeah, gacha is free - for the T-Dolls and Fairies.  Oh yeah, bet you had no idea about that from these pics.  But, once you get to the bad guy gacha?  Yeah, kiss that goodbye.  But then again, bad guys weren't worth a shit, if I recall correctly.
- Story starts off intriguing.  Slow, but intriguing.  But then, slowly devolves into writers attempting to channel Kojima and failing miserably at understanding why his brand of weirdness works.  It's basically "military industrial complex bad...also, M Night Shaymalan plot twists."  It got very strange and is part of why I ultimately stopped playing.
- Gameplay starts off simple, but not too bad - pretty satisfying making comps that roflstomp.  But, say goodbye to basic gameplay mechanics and say hello to ancient Drive docs that detail what a small bamboo vs large bamboo composition looks like and how you micromanage it at every stage if you want to start beating story AND collab/off-story events after roughly....*edit* Chapter 9, apparently, been gone a lot longer than I thought.  Been a long time, so I may be off, but yeah, interesting, fun, varied comps come to a hard stop after then.  At that point, you better get used to seeing the same 10, sometimes 15 T-Dolls if you want to make any progression.  A BIG reason for why I ultimately stopped playing - I didn't care I was bad at maneuvering my Dolls and lost because of it, I cared that I couldn't bring HK416 to basically any content because she did nothing to help me make progress.  Sorry, still have a soft spot for that character.
- See that pic of the T-Dolls standing in a spartan room with a tank coming down on the left?  Dorm room - people say there's no gacha, but those people are psychopaths who let their dolls stand in a barren room with no stimulation.  There's your gacha right there - you want cute little dorm rooms or at least something a bit more cheery to ease the PTSD of the battlefield, there's your gacha.
- Don't worry about materials gathering - once your account gets old enough, you'll literally hit all the caps on how much you can hold and you won't be able to spend the shit fast enough.
- I think of this as a positive, but ultimately up to you, a lot of the levelling up is time-based, so make sure to throw Dolls in whatever upgrade thing there is to throw them into.  If you're not min-maxing with time, you're wasting it, as far as the upgrade system goes.
- Kalina cute.
There's probably more, but these are the things that stand out the most at the time of writing this.  Ultimately, I still remember this game with a certain fondness, but as with all good things, couldn't last forever.  Maybe I'll keep this in my library to try and dig up my account from the depths of the Google Play graveyard and see what I've missed out on, but there's also reasons for why I ultimately stopped.

The nostalgic whiplash nulls my senses.  How long has it been since it all started?  Seven, eight years?  And yet, there has been nothing quite like it since.

Buckle up my friend.  The ramblings of a delusionally nostalgic commander aren't going to be short.  Some spoilers, nothing major past initial chapter.

Girls' Frontline (aka GFL, or "Dolls' Frontline" in Japan) is a gacha game from the golden age of gachas.  Before the times of Hoyoverse's reign, before Blue Archive shattered the Kancolle formula, and well before 3D gachas were all the rage.  This was the age of Kancolle clones, chibi characters in gameplay, and non-formulaic gacha systems.  It was a chaotic mess, but with all the soul that comes from such a product.

Let's start with the character designs and art.  Many of them are clearly simple and thematically focused (Stg44 wears a German uniform, Negev has several stars of David on her...).  These designs become more complex and subtle as GFL creates more characters to choose from, eventually reaching over four hundred standards, each with their own skins.  Some characters are even fan-made additions, such as AK74M.  The best part?  None of these characters require premium currency like modern gachas.  You don't pull for characters, you simply use harvestable resources from in game to build them.  The monetization is in the skins.

While I've heard people call the story art CGs "generic", I really don't know what they're talking about.  Unlike almost all of its competitors, GFL has a subdued, nearly undersaturated style that blends well with the bleak state of the story.

From the onset, the story's theme is notably darker than most anime is willing to go; [spoiler]you are introduced to the protagonist stuck in a chokehold, and immediately the plot demands sacrificial lambs[/spoiler].  It only gets more intense as the story progresses, with small bouts of levity to alleviate the pressure periodically.  But that's only for the first couple arcs of the story, and not what captivates so many readers.

The story shifts some time after the lead writers part ways (Yuzhong staying with GFL, [url=https://docs.google.com/document/d/1SPU1NIu8z7avwSDq3hpXLEyg64rBqbjCRKkX3fFBQyE/edit?tab=t.0]Yao Meng going on to create Arknights[/url]).  What was once a gradually developing plot boils over into a rollercoaster of desperate protagonists fighting against overwhelming odds, all while the elites conduct shrewd political intrigue and vie for control of the future of humanity.  The lore and prose drastically improve in this time, and I found myself completing entire story events designed to run weeks in a single day.

Take notice to how I've not talked about the gameplay yet.  That's because it's definitely the weakest link, and is for almost every MICA game.  It's a mix of auto-battler and turn-based strategy, but then also jury-rigged suddenly puzzle sequences?!  This is before even mentioning the spaghetti code that drives most character skills in GFL.  Curiously, the actual damage calculations and team-building is really fun and complex.  It is a shame that GFL never figured out what it wanted to do with the gameplay part of its game.

Honorable mention to the music and community, which both have an eternal impact on my life to this very day.

"...There's no place for you in this era. Know when to let go and make a timely exit."

Honestly, I'm just glad I got to be a part of GFL in its heyday.  Would I recommend it now?  Not really, no.  I would HIGHLY recommend finding the [url=https://gfstory-en.pages.dev/simulator?story=startavg%2Fstart0.txt]full GFL story[/url] online though.

For just being a game about girls with guns, Girls' Frontline sure did a lot more than I ever would have expected.  But its time is coming to an end.  The IP might go on, but GFL itself will run its last event sooner or later.

May this classic rest in peace.

I feel like, ahhh... It's always hard to write something meaningful into these reviews, like what do I really say when most of my valuation of a particular thing is fueled by just the nostalgia factor that I have? Obviously that is not really an objective signal of quality, nor it is relatable to others in any way shape or form.

As far as more objective evaluation goes, this is one of the first initial gachas out there, its monetization is infinitely less predatory than present day gachas. I own hundreds of characters, and I can still keep getting more as a total 100% free to player. Many of these characters are meta top tier picks, so its not like f2ps are getting showered with crap.
The literal only thing that is more substantially paywalled is just cosmetics, but you get an actually fairly generous trickle of the premium currency to allow you to occasionally spend on some costumes here and there, as well as get practical upgrades.

I do feel it's important to mention, yes there are practical upgrades locked behind premium currency; however you get enough premium currency at a decent enough rate that you will never really run dry on stuff. Such upgrades are barrack slots for more character capacity, equipment storage capacity, dormitories to showcase furniture sets, etc.
So, while practical none of these are actually impactful of gameplay beyond some nifty QoL degree of things, and you can always buy more storage for chars, equips when needed.

I am a long time vet of Girls Frontline, playing since the VA-11 Hall-A collab in 2019.
In short, if you want to play a rather generous gacha/kancolle game with a well written story that has unfortunately fallen off in recent times, I recommend this game.

In Long.
[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
Girls Frontlines gameplay is mostly servicable, it is not bad, it is not fantastic. Higher difficulty event maps can be a challenge, but for an established player, most things are not difficult.
The gameplay does shine when doing Ranked maps during events though, turning into a highly tactical game of judging what will get you the most points during your run. These are sadly few and far between, but whenever they do come about they are very fun. However, if you want to have multiple strong teams, you will likely have to grind as a new player. There is a good new player catch up system that helps you get a few good teams to start with though.

[h2] Story [/h2]
Once you get past the very poor beginnings of the story, into the more complex, action thriller style later chapters (CH10/Singularity onwards) and events, the story becomes very well done. In my opinion, the story is the strongest point of Girls Frontline, however, it has dropped in quality in recent events in part due to needing to wrap up threads because of Girls Frontline 2 and the writers being unable to do so in a coherent, believable and quality way. Becoming convoluted and unfocused, it is still decent and they don't take away from the previous chapters too much. I have my own gripes with the later story, but won't rant here about them.

[h2] Monetisation [/h2]
It is easily possible to play Girls Frontline entirely F2P and experience everything. Friends can help you clear maps by borrowing their echelons and getting characters is very easy. What Girls Frontline does monetise is the things that make the game less of a pain to deal with (more echelon slots, more doll slots etc) and Skins. It is possible to earn the currency used for these for free, but it is slow going. I am never a fan of gacha monetisations, but GF1s monetisation is very fair in my opinion.

[h2] Characters [/h2]
People play gacha for the characters and there is a large, but mostly shallow cast here. Some characters get much deeper dives into their stories and motivation, but most are very shallow. They are still very cute and lovely though. The characters that get the most development are those that are featured in main events or in the main squads, with others getting minor spotlights or small stories related to their skins (unfortunately you need to get the skin to read these.)

The community of Girls Frontline is very welcoming and there are many guides, MICA has crafted a mostly great story and I do recommend people give it a shot.

This game is quite ancient and it shows, however it also lacks some of the features some modern new age gachas post Genshin Impact like the abysmal 50/50. As someone who has spent countless years playing the game I can say it is arguably one of the most F2P friendly gacha in existence, in terms of beating content that is.

For gameplay you assemble a team of 5 T-Dolls (Female androids who are named after and use the gun of their namesake) of varying rarities and types arranged in a 9 tile grid just like the numpad on a keyboard. Each gun type like Assault Rifles or SMGs have buff tiles that enhance certain gun types and have specific tile coverages depending on the T-Doll you use. In late game you can also deploy long range fire supports (HOCs), Armored support (Mobile Armor) and even playable enemy units (Coalition). You use skills with the 1 - 5 keys and for more advanced strategy you can even pause buffer to micro with the mouse.

In terms of content there is a lot of content and upgrades to do. Leveling and skilling T-dolls, Fairies, Coalition units, Fire Support Units and Mobile Armors, enhancing and calibrating equipment, main story, night maps, both major and minor story events and the Exploration game mode. Want end game content? Try your hand on older ranking maps for exclusive gear or the limited time Theatre mode.

Unlike other gachas all the T-dolls  are either constructed with resources (Same as Kantai Collection) or farmed repeatedly until they drop, although the Coalition units (Playable enemy units) unfortunately do require premium currency (Electronic Impulse)

The game's monetization is quite light as well. You can spent 5 bucks on the monthly gem pass or even 10 on the BP to get extra resources. My advice though: Save enough gems to buy Two (2) construction slots, Two (2) Repair slots and then dump the rest into getting extra Echelon slots and Dorms. 

Luckily for you the most egregious gacha system is shelling Furniture coins for Skins and Furniture set, an L2D skin if being extremely unlucky can cost up to $400 to exchange for it. You can also accrue Black Tickets from skin dupes to redeem for other skins, of which there is A LOT. 

I do recommend trying the game if you are curios, dailies don't take too much time and is generally a nice side game if you are tired of the latest gachas.

It's an old game, first made and released during a time when the videogame industry did not collectively converge to concepts like "live service", "50/50 gacha", "battle pass", etc.

Before I start yapping off the deep end, let me tl;dr the game's entire concept to you - it is a resource management game, a waifu collector game, a realtime strategy-style experience, and a visual novel all in one. If you're a VN reader, or a person with some level of interest in guns, maybe both, or if you want to try something different from games that copy Hoyoverse's model, then this game is worth trying.

You can compare and contrast this game's core concept to Kantai Collection - it shares the same resource management (sending teams out for resources, watching over your usage of them, acquisition of units via construction, etc.), appeal to military enthusiasts (KanColle with WW2 naval history, GFL with firearms across all eras except maybe pre-WW1), and some combat mechanics (send team(s) to a map, move them around nodes, each node may trigger a battle within the map). 

But where KanColle's gameplay is literally just spin the compass and let RNG take where it wants you to, GFL requires your active participation, it lets you decide where to deploy your teams, where to move around them, and you can even do some Starcraft-esque micro in battles to extend the lifespan of your dolls. GFL also blows its inspiration out of the water by adopting QoL changes much earlier than its counterpart. I've retired from KanColle around the time Iowa was first introduced into that game, so I don't know of any QoL updates it has had since then, but GFL is already ahead of the game by doing some core things differently, such as not needing to resupply teams every time they return from a resource gathering mission, and also GFL devs have historically shown a commitment to improving the game's QoL. They've released UI updates every once in a while, and they also made sweeping changes to the daily gameplay loop back in 2020 or so (I honestly forgot which year that update was), reducing the friction and burden a player needs to go through to finish dailies. Honestly, Japanese devs could never.

Girls Frontline is also a narrative driven game, with a story that ramps up from a simple "our android friends vs. their robots gone rogue" premise to a political thriller, unravelling the game's world along the way. New friends antagonists come and go, some even become recurring characters, and each one helps you get one step closer to the game's core conflict at large. That is not to say the game's world is cold and unfriendly to you, the Commander, though, there are also side stories that explore each T-doll and their unique personalities and circumstances, usually in a more lighthearted manner. We old-timers love to joke about "love and hope" with respect to Girls Frontline's storywriting, as the main story can get dark, painful, sometimes even intense, but there are also many moments of levity if you know where to find them. And there is a LOT of story content to go through, both in main story and in side content. Almost 10 years' worth of it. If this game was released as a pure VN instead, it would have enough material for 5 or even more entries into the franchise.

I have to be real with you though, if you're completely new to the franchise and are giving this game a try, expect an experience of a game that was first released between 2016-2018. Bugs, jank, misinput-prone menus, you name it. It is a game buried under almost a decade's worth of technical debt, so much that Sunborn focuses more of their efforts into new projects instead. What you will experience with this game is a peek at a much simpler time, before Sunborn aimed for higher commercial ambitions with Girls Frontline 2: EXILIUM. It's also still a live service game, so it will still demand a level of commitment from you, with dailies to clock in for, and the grind to build up your account into the endgame. I don't know how grindy the game currently is, but back in the day of us GFL1 old-timers, we had to run maps like 0-2 daily for at least an hour or two to level dolls. Today's gacha games are grindy because they want dollars from you, so they timegate your progress and subject you to the whims of RNG. Games of GFL's era were grindy because they want hours of your time from you, so materials can get scarce and you'll have to minmax your resource management while trying to progress your entire account further.

There is also a A LOT of auxiliary mechanics to the core T-doll collection/management gameplay, like HOCs, Coalition units, and even vehicles. Girls Frontline is a waifu gacha strategy game with a mix of turn-based strategy and real-time strategy.

Gameplay: top-down turn-based strategy with sidescrolling real-time strategy in combat.
Sound: Stylized gunfire, explosions and anime-style voice acting in lobby and in combat.
Music: A mix of electronic and dramatic choir to fit the scene (main lobby, cutscene, mission, etc)
Story: There is a main campaign divided into chapters with misisons.
Gacha: Free-to-roll using in-game resources to roll for new units. Different outfits can be applied to the 'Commander' avatar and T-dolls.

For example:
 Chapter 1 has 6 missions labeled 1-1 – 1-6 with 'normal difficulty
 There is also 'Emergency' difficulty and 'Night Battle'
 'Emergency' is harder than 'normal'
 'Night Battle' requires doll formations set up for nightfighting to be able to see ahead using equipment and pistol-class T-dolls.

Chapters can be completed with a Gold, silver or bronze rating. Sometimes a certain rating is required to progress to the next chapter.
There are cutscenes before and after the missions in the style of a visual novel with written dialoge (no voice acting).

Enemy types: Different units (friendly and enemy) have different strengths and weaknesses. You have to set up different formations to deal with different threats in battle. Such as AR formations, machine gun formations, heavy weapons (mortars, ATGMs, etc), rifle quads, etc).
Formations are set up in a 3x3 grid pattern. Place your squads in the formation so that their 'buff tiles' overlap with one another so squads recieve formation buffs in combat.

You can equip and level up your squads to make them more effective. This is ESSENTIAL for later chapters.

In adition to the main campaign (Combat Mission) there are cononical side chapters like 'Operation Cube+ 5.5', 'Arctic Warfare 7.5' and more.

Finally there have been event missions like crossovers of franchies in the past such as the VA-11 Hall-A crossover that had its own missions and characters from that game.

Verdict: Play it for the story and to kill time. Sunborn account is required.
You can play it on PC, Android and IOS.

Girls Frontline is a very unique game, it has a mix of aesthetics found in few other pieces of media, an ancient gacha system which is alien to the modern gacha landscape, and gameplay which cannot be found in any game on the market. I am a huge fan but I'll be a bit conservative with my praise. (i'm level 190+ btw)

[h1]Story 9/10[/h1]
The story of Girls Frontline is, and should be, the main appeal for most people who stick with the game. It is not just a game about anthropomorphic guns, it does away with that idea in its narrative right away and it becomes obvious that that was only used as a selling point when that genre of gachas was very popular. It starts off slow but after the early chapters it maintains a high quality standard in all aspects (non-specific spoiler) [spoiler]up until the very end. Sadly due to the ending I cannot give this game a perfect 10/10 even though the story up to that point is right on the cusp of a perfect score.[/spoiler]
The story of Girls Frontline is a story about politics, the clash between Globalism and Nationalism and what people on both sides will do to see their side prevail. But more than that it is a story about people in a harsh world trying to do what they can in any way they can to make the world a better place. it is a story about machines learning about humanity and what is worth protecting to them and what they are willing to do  to protect their friends.
Girls Frontline also bucks the traditional gacha game ML trend where every female character loves the main character unconditionally. The commander in Girls Frontline earns the respect he gets from his dolls, and those who he has not earned the respect of do not respect him. Characters do not just exist to be a part of his harem or some bullshit like that, they are their own people.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[h3]Your mileage may vary, but for me its a 9/10[/h3]
The gameplay in Girls Frontline is very unique, you will not find ANY game out there with the same gameplay. It takes two forms one is a top down turn based tactics layer where you position echelons efficiently to achieve an objective. This objective starts out (mind-numbingly) simple but as the events progress they get more complex and interesting. This map layer can be extremely complex such as in the games competitive PvE maps aka "Ranking Maps". These maps can have a level of strategic depth to movement which takes hours or days to understand. Despite playing the game for three years at this point I still am not a true master of upper level strategy on the turn based layer of the game.

The second layer of the combat is the real time battle portion. Your dolls each have their own unique set of skills which can be utilized in tandem to bring down foes. This level of combat requires that you understand teambuilding mechanics properly and can build an effective team of dolls to take on a specific opponent. A team which excels in one fight might be destroyed in another and knowing these matchups and being able to build the right team to fit the enemy formation is the core of this layer of combat. In addition to knowing how to teambuild you have to know how to move within battle. Dolls can be moved around during battle which can make enemies target certain dolls over others and certain dolls target certain enemies. It can also delay enemies firing and give more time to eliminate them before they kill you. This real time layer of combat requires both strong teambuilding and execution. Everything in the game can be beaten if you have the right team and the right execution. 

The reason that I mark this gameplay down to a 9/10 from a 10/10 however is due to balance on the real time layer of combat. Certain units ruin this element of combat by being so strong that they can defeat 99% of the game without needing to change teams or move around in battle at all. I would honestly recommend if you have a unit which just wins the game for you to bench them because they're just making the experience less fun. On the bright side, even if you do use overpowered units, the turn based tactical layer of combat remains interesting and compelling.

[h1]Gacha 10/10 (For A Gacha Game)[/h1]
Girls Frontline is hardly a gacha by modern standards. Characters are obtained via pulling on a pool of characters yes, but the resources to pull from this pool are easy to obtain and you are NEVER encouraged to pay for more of them and the conversion rate is so bad it would be absurd to pay. You get thousands of pulls a month. The drawback of this system is there is no pity for dolls. You could go a very long time without ever seeing a certain doll you really want. To help combat this issue all new players get two free "anchors" essentially they allow you to pick from a pool of most of the rarest craftable dolls in the game and guarantee one in a small amount of pulls. There is also a more traditional gacha for enemy characters but it is quite generous and you'll be able to obtain most useful characters very easily. It is still a gacha game, so it could be better.

[h1]Waifus 10/10[/h1]
I seem to be a bit of an anomaly in terms of gacha players, I don't actually play for waifus. I play for the story. I never download a gacha game just because I find a character hot. However I do think Girls Frontline has very strong designs and characters. The characters of course all use some kind of firearm, they can be as old as the Colt Walker pistol made in 1847 or as new as the RPK-16 light machine gun made in 2016. The characters all take inspiration from their firearms but they are not just anthropomorphized guns. While often inspired by the circumstances around the gun's development, all the characters are a part of the near future setting of Girls Frontline. All the dolls are more than just their firearm. Characters who are included in the story will get a lot of depth to their characters and all have their own motives for what they do and why they do it.

[h1]Guns 9/10[/h1]
They look good, you'll notice some errors but for the most part they're extremely faithful to what the guns look like in the real world and if you're a gun nut you'll enjoy seeing how well they're drawn. Occasionally there will be a gun which is miscategorized of however. Like for instance the semi auto only P50 pistol is classified as a submachine gun.
And just ignore gameplay as every gun fires like a semi auto except machine guns and only machine guns and shotguns reload.

[h1]Performance 9/10[/h1] 
I'd have listed it a lot earlier if it was a concern. Its an old game, and its not very visually ambitious. Constant QoL updates have put it into a very playable state but there are often bugs

[h1]Live Service 5/10[/h1]
[h3]Mica pls...[/h3]
The live service aspect of the game can vary greatly. for the past year the EN server had a pretty abysmal schedule however managment of the server has shifted and it has improved a lot so its too early to tell if its going to stay ok. I never expect great live service from these developers, but sometimes its REALLY bad. Fortunately the game is in a mostly complete state so its not dependent upon live service updates. I don't find the bad live service to be much of a deal breaker just cause there's already so much content in the game.

[h1]The Biggest Problem With The Game[/h1]
The biggest problem with the game is that new story events are not immediately added to the game as soon as they conclude. there can be a gap as long as 2 years or more between when a story even runs in a limited duration and when it is added to the permanent campaign. This is entirely an issue with the developers deciding to drip feed permanent content in order to fill out months with less limited event content. They have the ability to put all the events into permanent campaign immediately but choose not to

Temps are good on my system when the game is running, but everyone's rig is different. Game doesn't use that many resources and, according to task manager and other benchmarking tools, isn't even that intensive. On phones? Girls' Frontline back in the day ran like trash. Constant crashes. Overheating phones. Not even running properly on certain Android devices so players would miss out on events and story. The PC port? Like I said, decent port. Other elements tend to be rather blurry due to lack of upscaling (backgrounds during story, maps, etc.), which most gacha game PC ports seem to be unwilling to resolve. Big surprise. Oh, and there doesn't seem to be an exit game hotkey (that I know of as of writing this) to quit the game when you're finished like any other mobile game port on Steam. Mashed ESC button and nothing. Have to go into windowed mode to exit out the window or ALT + F4. Frustrating to say the least.

UI elements work through the cursor, but it's dumb. Clickable tabs will be lightly highlighted, but you still need to click the correct tab. Why not implement section by section tab selection via keyboard? Why not implement hotkeys for easier navigation? Why not implement custom cursors in the spirit of the game? Literal yellow bold cursor would make a huge difference vs default windows cursor. Seriously. Like dude, this is a port running on PCs now; we have actual peripherals to utilize. This port isn't for phones. Stupid is as stupid does. <_<

As far as story goes, I think the summary description provided on the game's page does a good job giving an idea of what to expect. And perhaps the best part of the game when it comes to the story is that all time limited story events eventually get added to archives, so there isn't any real reason to rush through the game's story. The stories, campaigns and events are long & difficult, but can be rather rewarding imo. Tutorials are decent and they've added a lot of 'new player' friendly stuff in the past few years (...which again, should've been added during the early days of the game's lifecycle...). I remember when everything was barebones and people just kinda figured things out on their own. And hey, there's plenty of guides online if you ever get stuck. All made by members of the community. Like I always say, the biggest reason this game even got as far as it did was the community's unbridled passion for pretty much every aspect of the game rather than useless nonsense, which is something the Girls' Frontline '2' will never have nor understand.

Battles are line battles with grid elements. You barely do anything early game aside from setting your formations and moving your units accordingly to the enemy's formation and attacks. Late game stages get complicated, but as you progress, you essentially learn the game and it shouldn't be a problem. Teams/squads actually have to work TOGETHER instead of having 416/AK-15 do all the work. Tutorials in game explain the basics. Your job is to supplement the basics and pull through. It is ultimately up to the player to think outside the box and strategize through trial and error. You're a commander, after all. Not a gacha slave. Strategy is one of the elements that is truly make or break for some people and ultimately the deciding factor if the game is for them or not.

One of the main draws of the game aside from the story is that you do not have to spend any money at all to progress.  It is extremely player friendly. Very ANTI instant gratification, if you will. All characters (aside from collaboration time limited ones) are either craftable or farmable through map clear drops. Characters recruited or 'crafted' through the factory use a mix of four different in game resources to build. And with a roster of over 400 characters, paying real money for crafting tickets PLUS the resources required to even attempt crafting is economically/statistically unfeasible and a huge reason why no one does it in the first place. We all just played the game instead of auto battling or hitting the stage sweep button in an instant. Time investment and patience is biggest gatekeep when it comes to Girls' Frontline. Everyone who has played since launch until today most likely has every single doll by now with enough resources to to eventually craft/build up any new characters that would eventually come out. In game currency is also decently plentiful as you gain achievements and clear campaign stages. Saving up what you can and being smart in what you spend currency on is key in any gacha after all.

Girls’ Frontline is very similar to Plants vs. Zombies, it’s a survival/tower defense game where you collect and upgrade guns personified as female anime cyborgs. As the commander, you send these “gun girls” on defensive missions to stop a sentient robotic race trying to wipe out humanity. The game has a steep learning curve, so I wouldn’t recommend it to beginners. New players often run out of a key resource called Dummy Cores, which are required for Dummy Link. Without them, progression can grind to a halt. I highly suggest reading up on Core Hell before diving in.

The UI is messy and feels overwhelming at first, but it’s manageable once you spend time exploring it. This game is very text-heavy, so if you’re not a fan of reading, it might not be your style. Another minor annoyance is the naming scheme for characters. While guns like Scorpion, Grizzly, and Thompson are easy to remember, names like G11, OTs-14, WA2000, and LWMMG are much harder to recall, which can make discussing characters with friends tricky.

Gameplay wise, every mission puts you on the defensive. You won’t be charging into enemy bases or blasting everything heroically; it’s essentially tower defense, reminiscent of Space Marine in Warcraft 3 or Plants vs. Zombies. Your units hold positions and shoot waves of enemies, which can feel repetitive.

Visually, the game is inconsistent. The maps are cartoonish and look like they’re aimed at children, which contrasts sharply with the game’s serious tone. Character sprites also feature large “bubble heads,” a chibi style that doesn’t fit the darker atmosphere. Combat visuals and the paper style overworld maps also don’t match, which breaks immersion. Despite these flaws, the writing, character design, and tower defense gameplay are solid. The developer’s customer service is excellent, and overall, the game provides a fun, strategic experience.

Good afternoon. I'm here to drop a review/summary of the game, as someone who's been playing since 2018.

As such:

-From a technical viewpoint, the port is infinitely superior to running an emulator (at least, LDPlayer, which is what I had been using). The only downside is the lack of hotkeys. Otherwise, just do yourself a favor and play it via Steam.

-Economy wise, the game takes KanColle's base and vastly iterated and improved it over a decade. Going one by one, you have the following gameplay elements:

.- Dolls (the units themselves); crafted via resources farmed passively. You'd have to be a fool to purchase them.
.- Equipment; same as dolls.
.- Fairies (extra buffs); same as dolls and equipment, but more of a later game thing.
.- HOC's (special units that provide fire support); you get some as base, then can unlock extras by doing research. They use batteries and the research resource for such. Batteries are generated via dorms.
.- Protocol Assimilation units: Basically, hostile units made to fight for you. The one element that handles in a way that's closer to modern gachas. There's a pool of 100 units, one of which is the ringleader (boss/command units). You have normal pulls, extra pulls, and tickets. Normal pulls generate passively, with a cap of 14 at a time. 
Extra pulls behave the same, except you earn them and they can stack indefinitely. Both have to deal with RNG chances of acquiring whatever it is they're targeting (guaranteed for a basic unit, 50/50 for an intermediate one, 1/4 for a ringleader.
.- Tank/Mech: Researched and obtained purely via in game means.
Tickets bypass this check, but they carpet bomb (both figuratively and literally) the roster. So, for example, if you have 10 units left in the pool, and use 5 tickets, it's a flip coin chance whether it'll secure the ringleader.
.- Infraestructure: Doll/equipment/echelon/dorm/etc slots. All bought, but passive gems income is quite generous, so you don't really need to splurge if you don't want to.
.- Skin/gacha: The only real gacha in this game, and it's cosmetic. And you can earn the currency for it over time, with a common strategy being to save up a bunch of tokens and get several skins in a specific banner, and then get black cards, which can be used to redeem most skins.

.- Gameplay wise, the basic gist of it is that you can put together echelons, comprising of either Assault Rifles (generalist DPS), Rifles (High penetration, longer ranged DPS), Submachine Guns (tanks), Handguns (buffers), Machine Guns (burst DPS), or Shotguns (armored tanks). Do note that the descriptions are *exceptionally* broad, and in reality, there are loads of niches within each class. You'll need to do your own research for specific units.

Once you've done that, you use them on any given map/mission to carry out the objective. Sounds simple enough, but GFL1 has a deceptively extraordinary amount of depth going on for its gameplay, especially earlier on, and especially with some of the puzzle maps that it has. 

If that's of interest for you, and if you want a nominally gacha game that you can play while not really caring about stamina (other than the very early game, I suppose), then it'll probably be a rather interesting game for you. Though, I'd note that the game's mainly known for its story, which is going to be my next point.

.- Story wise, the game's main story has already concluded on CN, while EN/Global is waiting for the final trio of events. It starts slow for the first tranche (up to arguable chapter 8 or so), but it certainly speeds up by Chapter 10/Singularity. Which sounds really late, but this content originally came out in late 2019. 

Which is to say, relatively early on its lifespan. From there, it goes up and down on intensity, with a final bit (chapter 15) which, for a number of reasons, was unfortunately not that great. It's my understanding that this was remedied, to some extent, via the aforementioned trio of events (which serve as epilogues), but I can't give my firsthand impressions thereof, givent hat EN hasn't gone through them yet.

With that in mind, the story worth delving into? I'd say yes, provided that you have about a weeks' worth of spare time (this is not an exaggeration; that's probably the amount of time that it'd take to go through the story. You can, and absolutely should, take it slowly). It's my opinion that the good far outweighs the bad and middling. I also think that the story is the main thing that you'd play it for (that's certainly the case for me).

With that being said, there *are* cutscene interpreters thatt virtually turn GFL1 into a VN of sorts, bypassing the gameplay elements. How does that weigh up against playing the game and going through the cutscenes that way? 

I'd say that it depends on whether you like the gameplay at all. If not, then I'd say go that route. If yes, I'd say play it. I'd actually recommend playing up to Singularity either way, because early on, gameplay and story were far more intertwined (the story began before the gameplay section, and ended afterwards; sometimes, bit played during it), meaning that a VN experience would be jarring for such. They eventually made it so that gameplay and story nodes were fully separated, bypassing that issue.

Either way, it's my view that GFL1's story is one that's worth experiencing, and combine that with the fact that the port was done competently, I'm giving it a positive review.

The actual gameplay, aside from micromanaging all your 'T-Dolls' (your anime girls), is you basically move squads of these girls around a map, between nodes, and your goal is to clear the map as soon as possible while fulfilling certain criteria. The story is somewhat notable because it's pretty dark and arguably the bad guys are kind of in the right, but as far I remember the story really started to get muddy, in that the 'bad guys actually good guys' were doing some pretty horrific things to their own allies, and then I started to kind of lose interest in the game, I think. Had this port been released two or three years ago, this game would have received a glowing recommendation from me.

Unfortunately, times have changed, and not for the better. MICA has since gone to sap away every ounce of goodwill they have built up over the years, and thousands of users and several longtime content creators are now abandoning ship en-masse and rightfully so, from a combination of bad business decisions (Though mostly contained to GFL 2), leaving global out to dry regarding content, and the lead writer's own hackery regarding the story.

The gameplay is...there. Battles are mainly stat/level checks, with both sides standing and shooting at each other until the other one drops, with some limited input from the player mainly in the form of an exploit known as "kiting" - moving a unit to the front so the enemies will stop and aim at it before immediately withdrawing it back to the middle column and forcing the enemy to move again, buying you a couple extra seconds before the enemy starts shooting at you while your units chip away at them as they run towards you. It's not bad, but it's not anything you're going to find yourself booting up the game just to experience either. 

The real draw of the game used to be the story, even if it starts out pretty slow. The story in the first seven or so chapters is fairly non-existent, cutscenes only being a couple minutes long at the most and only really serving to establish context for the gameplay levels. It is only around Chapter 10 where the game shifts gears into a full blown Visual Novel and starts to get good. The game takes sudden, dark, and intense turn while more and more details about the setting are revealed, becoming a straight up survival horror game at times while you and your companions try to navigate your way through this menacing conspiracy between two factions that could crush you like a bug if you make one wrong move. This is where the game truly shines, coming to a head in the event Polarized Light where you are forced to make a desperate stand against the odds while it feels like the whole world comes down on top of you.

But wait, you ask, why am I giving this a negative review, then?

Because, unfortunately, Polarized Light is where this game peaks, and it is all downhill from there, kids. Oh boy oh boy, it is *all* downhill.

The story gets progressively sillier, and sillier from there, introducing a new primary Villain by the name of William, who is an absolute clown that the game cannot decide whether he is supposed to be menacing or not. One moment, it's pulling back the veil to reveal him as a hack fraud coasting by on Daddy's money who backstabbed his way to the top, and then in another it's frantically trying to throw the veil back on and acting like you're supposed to fear him and what he's capable of. The worst part about this is that due to MICA's insistence on tying this game in with another game, Reverse Collapse, William is given full plot armor despite being a constant presence as the primary villain, stopping him being the driving emotional force behind the narrative. The Elite Nytos, who stand in for the Sangvis Ferri Ringleaders in Act 3 of the story, fall into the exact same pitfalls as the Ringleaders did during Act 1, absolutely hamming up every scene and whenever an opportunity comes to fight them and make any forward progress in the story, the game will either unironically drop *It was a hologram* or *turns invisible and flies away* in a cutscene immediately after defeating them. Compared to the story we got in Act 2, it falls short on every front and falls squarely back into the failings of Act 1 despite a sect of the fanbase living in ardent denial of this, somehow praising Act 3 while badmouthing Act 1 in defense of it.

But the real kicker of why this gets a negative from me comes in Chapter 15, which goes beyond falling short and unfortunately puts the game on the same pedestal as the likes of Mass Effect 3 and Game of Thrones Season 8, where we drop plot twists into the mix that are so bad that they retroactively ruin every event prior, and then even go on to preemptively ruin any and all future stories that could ever be told in this universe, going from what was once a fairly grounded post-apocalyptic war story/geopolitical thriller to pulling supernatural elements out of its ass while wedging itself firmly up the writers, the plot disappearing under a mountain of purple-prose author self-fellatio. Beloved characters are cast aside if they're lucky, the unlucky ones are character assassinated or become the subject of outright torture porn.  Also, much like Mass Effect 3, the game's ending ended up being so bad and received so poorly, that the developers even had to go back and add in a whole new epliogue of events which, unfortunately, also like Mass Effect 3, only gave a marginal at best improvement.

It's a real shame, too. The character artwork is nice, and the soundtrack is excellent, but there is plenty of fanart you can indulge in without subjecting yourself to an online casino, and the game's soundtrack is available on youtube.

The only other plus this game has in 2025 is that it is still extremely F2P friendly, *especially* for a gacha game, but that doesn't matter, because this game will rob you of something much more finite, precious, and irreplaceable than money.

If you are a newcomer and you aren't someone who still thinks that Bioshock: Infinite was the pinnacle of human achievement with absolutely nothing wrong with it, your time is much better spent elsewhere, and there are plenty of other companies more deserving of your money.
